column4: The section reads the root of 88:1's “came” as a camel's forelegs moving in a walk. Here lean camels bring pilgrims from every distant pass; the dictionary gait becomes an actual caravan arrival.

The section's lexical note identifies مَصْفُوفَة as rows of sacrificial camels; this ayah has camels standing صَوَافَّ as God's name is recalled, then directs eating and feeding the content and the asker. Ordered camels, remembrance, and provision meet in one rite.

The section sets the nearby camel against far sky, mountains, and earth, and develops the animal as a carrier. This verse says livestock carry loads to a distant land people could not reach without great strain, making the camel's everyday closeness tangible.

The section's journey lexicon describes a full day of travel followed by camping at night. This verse pictures livestock being brought home in the evening and sent out in the morning, giving that daily rhythm a concrete herd scene.

The section's root note for تُسْقَى (س ق ي) includes a waterskin for water and milk. Here God gives people pure, easy-to-swallow milk from between waste and blood, showing the camel's milk-and-waterskin vocabulary against a startling account of animal provision.

The section explicitly links its word for milk that goes down easily, سَائِغًا in 16:66, with the swallowing root in this ayah. The condemned person gulps the boiling drink but can hardly swallow it, reversing the section's image of drink made easy for the recipient.

The section follows camel milk from udder to cup. This ayah calls livestock a lesson, says people are given drink from their bellies, and names their other benefits and meat; it makes milk one part of the animal's broad provision.
After 23:21 names milk and the livestock's benefits, this neighboring verse says people are carried on animals and ships. It supplies the transport side of the camel's usefulness in the section.

The section's lexical note connects نَاعِمَة to نَعَم, livestock, and to blessing. This verse names al-anʿām as created for warmth, benefits, and food, grounding that wordplay in the practical good the animals provide.

The section names 88:3's عَامِلَة as a root with a branch describing a working camel. Here the root occurs in “what Our hands have worked” to describe God's creation of livestock for people; work shifts from the exhausted faces to the Creator's making.

The section presents the camel as a familiar useful creature. This verse says the animals were made serviceable for people, who ride some and eat some, directly spelling out two of the camel's ordinary benefits.
The section tracks milk and its delivery in vessels. This continuation says the livestock provide other benefits and drinks, extending the camel's bodily provision beyond food and riding.

The section says the camel helps furnish the room. This verse names animal hides for houses and their wool, camel hair, and other hair for furnishings and use, making the dwelling's animal materials explicit.

The section brings camel milk together with cups and the camel as a carrier. In Yusuf's story, the missing royal cup is paired with a reward of a camel's load; the ayah joins vessel and caravan measure in a distinct scene.
The section's camel is a humanly near asset, and its dictionary discussion includes riding. This verse says God made livestock so people can ride some and eat some, stating the paired use directly.

The section describes the camel as a carrier and source of benefit. This verse names further benefits, carrying needs on livestock and ships, so it broadens the camel's role from food and riding to transport.
The section develops the camel as a mount. This verse says God made livestock and ships as mounts, directly placing animal travel beside sea travel.

The section's camel is both a creature to observe and a blessing people use. This verse says riders should settle on the animals' backs and remember their Lord's favor, connecting the mount to gratitude.

After the section cites the camel sacrifice in 22:36, this neighboring Hajj verse says to eat from the livestock offering and feed the distressed poor. It supplies the distribution of sacrificial food in its own passage.

The section presents the camel as useful wealth and names rows of sacrificial camels. This Hajj verse says the sacrificial animals benefit people for a set term before their destination is the Ancient House, joining practical use to the offering's endpoint.

The section pairs sacrifice with naming God and feeding people in 22:36. This neighboring ayah says neither the animals' flesh nor blood reaches God, but piety does; it clarifies what the feeding and sacrifice signify.

The section glosses الإبل as camels and as a form of wealth. This verse explicitly names الإبل among paired livestock, then asks which sex God supposedly forbade; it places the camel herd inside a concrete argument about animal food and its limits.
The section's camel can subsist on fresh growth without needing to drink first. Here the people of the Fire drink like thirsty camels, reversing that image into desperate, unrelieved thirst.

The section contrasts the easy drink of milk with the afterlife's harsh drink. This verse says the people of the Fire drink boiling water after their food, giving the scene of thirst its own punishing beverage.

The section sets an animal that can be satisfied by little fresh growth against people whose food fails them. This ayah assigns the people of the left the fruit of the Zaqqūm tree, an afterlife food scene on the opposite side of that contrast.

The section contrasts an animal's modest grazing with people left unsatisfied in 88:6–7. This verse says the condemned fill their bellies from the Zaqqūm, making the quantity of food no remedy for the torment.
The section explains that the cups in paradise can hold milk. This ayah depicts cups passed among the blessed from a flowing spring, a close parallel between the promised cup and its source.
The section describes cups set out in a garden with a flowing spring. This verse calls the drink white and delightful to drinkers, giving the promised beverage its pleasant quality.

The section places cups among the garden's furnishings and says no idle speech is heard there. This ayah depicts the blessed passing a cup among themselves with neither idle speech nor sin, joining the cup scene to the garden's quiet.

The section's garden has a running spring and placed cups, while its other scene has an un-swallowable drink in Hell. This description contrasts the two destinations through rivers of fresh water and milk, and boiling water for the Fire's people.

The section explains its garden cups through the image of vessels being filled from a camel's milk. This ayah's garden has cups, pitchers, and a cup from a flowing spring, making the vessel-and-drink scene explicit.
The section's cups belong to the garden's provision. This ayah says the righteous drink a cup mixed with camphor, giving a specific drink to set beside the section's offered cups.
The section joins cups to a flowing spring. This verse says the righteous drink from a spring that God's servants make flow, supplying the source behind a garden cup.
The section's cup imagery includes vessels arranged in the garden. This ayah describes silver vessels and cups passed around, furnishing a direct parallel for placed cups.
The section describes a cup as a vessel for milk. This ayah names a cup mixed with ginger in the garden, giving another concrete drink carried by a cup.
The section's garden includes a running spring beside its cups. This ayah identifies a spring named Salsabil, completing the drink's source in its own scene.
The section pictures a garden furnished with cups. This ayah has golden platters and cups carried around among the blessed, a direct parallel in the arrangement of garden vessels.

The section's camel lexicon describes an animal sustained by fresh growth rather than water. This verse says God brought water and pasture from the earth, naming the two parts of that provision together.

The section treats the camel as a creature kept by provision and made useful to people. This verse calls what came before provision for people and their livestock, giving grazing animals a place in the creation scene.
The section asks the reader to look at the camel as a nearby created sign. This ayah likewise commands a look, directing attention to human food; it makes eating itself an object of reflection.
The section's camel can live on fresh growth. This ayah names fruit and herbage among the earth's produce, bringing grazing growth into the food sequence.

The section develops the camel as an animal sustained by what grows and useful to people. This ayah calls the preceding food a provision for people and their livestock, explicitly joining human and animal sustenance.

The section describes a camel that can subsist on moist growth without first drinking. This verse sends down water for people to drink and says vegetation grows where livestock graze, linking water, pasture, and the animal's nourishment.

The section treats the camel as a mount and carrier. This neighboring livestock passage names horses, mules, and donkeys for riding and adornment, placing the camel's transport role among other created mounts.
The section's camel is sustained by pasture. This verse says rain brings forth varied plants and directs people to eat and let their livestock graze, directly naming the animal's food.

The section follows the camel's relation to water and grazing. This verse describes rain sent to revive dead land and to provide drink for livestock and many people, joining animal thirst to renewed pasture.

The section says the camel can be satisfied by fresh growth. This verse describes water reaching barren land and crops that people and their livestock eat, setting out the provision on which grazing depends.
The section's root note describes camels and wild animals getting by on fresh growth. This verse says God brought out the pasture, naming the plant world at the center of that lexical image.

The section's camel is shown beside the far sky, mountains, and earth as a sign to look at. This ayah also asks people to look at the sky above and how it was built, extending the same gaze from nearby creature to distant creation.

The section sets the camel's familiar body against mountains and the spread earth. This verse names the spread earth and firmly placed mountains, closely paralleling the surrounding landscape of its gaze.

The section moves from looking at created signs to the command to remind. This ayah says the sky and earth scene is insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back, linking observation to remembrance.

The section places the camel as an ordinary creature close to human life just after describing a garden. This ayah says the deniers will not enter the Garden until a camel passes through a needle's eye, using the same animal to mark an impossible boundary to entry.
The section sets a camel in view alongside the hot Fire scene. This ayah likens the Fire's sparks to yellow camels, making the animal itself the scale and shape of a fiery image.

The section asks the reader to look at the created camel and notes its relation to pasture. In this account, the she-camel is God's sign and is left to eat on God's earth; the animal's grazing becomes a test of how people treat a provision.

The section links the camel to grazing and sustenance. This account also commands the people to leave God's she-camel to eat from God's earth, then warns them not to harm her; it presents animal provision as something humans must respect.

The section's camel is an animal whose water needs are unusual and whose milk is carried. This account assigns God's she-camel a set day to drink and the people their own day, making access to water the exact point of the sign.

After the camel's water turn is specified in 26:155, this verse warns the people not to touch her with harm. It reverses the section's attentive regard for the camel into a scene where people violate the sign.
The section treats the camel itself as a sign to be observed. This ayah calls the she-camel a trial and commands the audience to watch, giving the animal a testing role as well as a created one.
The section develops the camel's relation to water and drinking. This verse says the water is apportioned among the people and the she-camel, making the animal's drink a matter of shared measure.

The section asks readers to regard the camel and recalls its dependence on pasture rather than frequent water. This ayah names God's she-camel and its turn to drink, foregrounding the animal's access to water.
The section's camel is a creature to be contemplated and provisioned. This ayah says the people hamstrung God's she-camel, turning regard for the animal into its violent opposite.
The section places the camel in a landscape of distant mountains. This neighboring ayah says God set the mountains firmly in place, extending the same creation scene around the camel and pasture.
